Slavonski Brod Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Slavonski Brod, Croatia

Not demolished. Slavonski Brod, a Sava River border town near Bosnia with Roman roots (ancient Marsonia), spent 150 years under Ottoman rule from 1536 before becoming an important Austrian military and later civil administrative center by the mid-19th century. Jews arrived from Hungary and Slovakia in the 19th century - only 2 residents by 1857, growing to 287 by century's end and formally organizing in 1873. A striking 1896 synagogue, designed by Leo Hönigsberg and Julius Deutsch, was considered one of the empire's most beautiful before its 1941 destruction. Despite generally amicable community relations, local Croats proved highly active in wartime antisemitic violence; of 750 regional Jews before the war, only 10 survived. Rabbi Leib Weissberg was deported to Jasenovac and killed in 1942, alongside many congregants; a few Brod Jews joined Tito's partisan resistance. Only 16 Jews remained by 1961. This cemetery, built in 1880 and later confiscated by the state in 1958, retains its original brick wall and gate, the Cohen family mausoleum, and its 1880 ceremonial hall (renovated in 2015); tombstones span 1894 to 2015, in Hebrew, German, Hungarian, and Croatian.
